title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context (from p.163): Euler had modelled a vertical column of unit weight per length bending under its own weight. The abscissa AX = x is measured downward from the top A, and the deflection is XY = y. Taking moments about the section at X of the weight of the part above gives ∫_0^x ξ dy(ξ) + E y''(x) = 0. This is the integrated form of the modern equation EI y''' + w x y' = 0. The top conditions are y(0)=0 and y''(0)=0 (no moment at a free top), with slope y'(0)=A. Writing u = y' gives E u'' + x u = 0, an Airy-type equation. Its power-series solution 1 − x^3/(2·3E) + 1·4 x^6/(2···6 E^2) − … integrates to Euler's series y/A = x − x^4/(2·3·4E) + 1·4x^7/(2···7E^2) − … . In modern form u ∝ √x J_{−1/3}((2/3)x^{3/2}/√E). The curve has infinitely many extrema, all apparently on one side of the axis, which had first led Euler to think columns could be made arbitrarily tall without failing.

This page: Euler says he has since shown 'from other principles' (the companion papers) that every column strength has a definite limiting height. He then diagnoses the paradox. The equation is correct, since it comes from sound equilibrium principles, but it assumes the top A is entirely free of any force and may move sideways. The question of the limiting height of a column, however, presupposes that both A and the foot B are held on the same vertical line, a pinned–pinned type condition. If the free top is kept, nothing in the 'wonderful curve' is absurd: cases can always be found that agree with it.

Section 3 (begun here, continued on p.165) replaces the column by an elastic lamina of equal stiffness and reads each arc AY as an equilibrium shape under self-weight. The lamina is clamped at Y in the direction of its tangent there. At the extrema of y the tangent is vertical, so the lamina can be planted vertically in the floor. That is exactly a vertical cantilever, clamped at the base and free at the top, buckling under self-weight. Its smallest length is the first zero of u, x^3/E ≈ 7.84, i.e. l ≈ 1.986 (EI/w)^{1/3} (Greenhill's flagpole value).
errors: No mathematical error on this page. Euler's diagnosis is right: the original equation and series encode a free top end (zero shear and moment) and are correct for that case. They simply do not answer the question with the top held on the vertical.

The implicit earlier error (p.163) was interpretive. Taking the first maximum of y as a clamped base, the free-top problem itself has a critical height: the first extremum. Euler had wrongly read the curve as allowing unlimited height.

ideas.what: Equilibrium equation for a heavy elastic column bending under its own weight, E y'' + ∫_0^x ξ dy = 0, i.e. E y''' + x y' = 0, with series solution
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1778–80 for the equation; Greenhill 1881 for the correct critical height via Bessel functions
ideas.where_published: E510 itself and the companion column papers in Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1778 (pars I, publ. 1780); discussed by Truesdell (Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies, OO II.11.2)

ideas.what: Diagnosis of the 'paradox' of infinite column height: it depends on the boundary condition at the top (free vs. held on the vertical line AB)
ideas.modern_name: Dependence of the buckling eigenvalue on boundary conditions (cantilever vs. pinned–pinned)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (self-correction in E510); generally treated in Euler's own 1744 elastica classification for end-loaded columns
ideas.where_published: E510; companion 'Examen insignis paradoxi' paper (exact E-number unsure)

ideas.what: Replacing a column by an elastic lamina of equal stiffness, and reading each arc of the solution curve as the equilibrium shape of a lamina clamped at an arbitrary point (vertically at the extrema)
ideas.modern_name: Equivalence of the linear eigenvalue problem with clamped-free self-weight buckling (flagpole problem); critical length from the first zero of a J_{−1/3}-type function
ideas.usually_credited_to: Greenhill 1881 (critical height of a vertical pole / tree)

missed.claim: Euler's construction amounts in principle to the clamped-base, free-top self-weight buckling solution, usually credited to Greenhill (1881). Clamping the lamina at the first extremum of the curve, i.e. the first zero of the Airy-type series y', gives the critical height. This is known to Euler scholars (Truesdell), so it is likely not new. Still, engineering histories often say flatly that 'Euler failed and Greenhill solved' without noting that Euler's own series and clamping argument already contain the cantilever case.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only for historical credit in structural-stability textbooks. The mathematics is fully established.

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's self-diagnosis of the self-weight column paradox through boundary conditions. It is documented in E510 and discussed by Truesdell. The near-anticipation of Greenhill's flagpole result is mildly interesting but already noted in the specialist literature.
transcription_corrections: 'proquaerimus' probably reads (or should read) 'perquirimus' in the print; the scan is ambiguous.
Line-break hyphenations ('quo-vis', 'poſ-ſe', 'ſuccum-berent', 'vi-rium', 'praetermittere-tur', 'ſubſti-tui') should be joined: quovis, poſſe, ſuccumberent, virium, praetermitteretur, ſubſtitui.
